title: PlanningReady: Australian Capital Territory (approval pathways)
notes: First sourced rules for the ACT, territory-wide. The ACT has no councils: the ACT Government (Territory Planning Authority, ACT Planning, Access Canberra) is the planning authority. references.section: Check if you're exempt from a DA
references.extracted_text: [Summary, not the source's wording] Some projects don't need a development application if they meet the general criteria and the specific criteria in Schedule 1 of the Planning (Exempt Development) Regulation 2023. General criteria cover significant development, essential design elements, easements, plumbing and drainage, tree protection, environment, heritage, the crown lease, dwelling numbers and loose-fill asbestos. Examples of exempt categories include carports, pergolas, courtyard walls, demolition of single dwellings, driveways, fences up to 2.3 m in most cases, garages and sheds, solar and heating, home businesses within limits, decks, pools, water tanks up to 20 kL and single dwellings with conditions such as neighbour notification. Exempt work must still meet other laws including the Building Act 2004. A building certifier can give a formal exemption notice; the DA Gateway Team gives advice but not exemption approvals. Minor non-compliance may be covered by an exemption declaration.
references.interpretation: Many single dwellings and minor works are exempt from a DA, but we can't check the Schedule 1 criteria, so a DA is MAY_APPLY. Captured on 2026-10-12 from an automated summary of the published page; the exact wording was not available. references.extracted_text: [Summary, not the source's wording] DAs are submitted through eDevelopment after registering with the Application for Access to Electronic Services. Applications need documents meeting the minimum documentation requirements, a letter of authorisation, a Development Outcomes Report (required for all DAs), a design response where applicable, and a greenhouse gas emissions statement if required. The application is checked for completeness, fees are paid, and it is then formally lodged. DA Gateway Team: 02 6205 2888, planningenquiries@act.gov.au.

references.extracted_text: [Summary, not the source's wording] Decision timeframes in working days: standard development 30 with no representations, 45 with representations; significant development 60; concurrent DAs 10 after the concurrent process. Public notification is 15 working days for most DAs, and two stages of 20 and 10 working days for significant development.

references.extracted_text: [Summary, not the source's wording] The Territory Plan is the key tool of the ACT's outcomes-focused planning system. The authority can give advice on proposals before a DA is lodged. Lodgement triggers public notification and entity referrals; the ACT Heritage Council and the Emergency Services Agency are possible referral entities. Most building work requires building approval under the Building Act 2004, assessed by private building certifiers. Development approval generally expires five years after it takes effect. Lease variation approvals generally end once the lease is varied or 2 years after the approval took effect. You can ask for reconsideration, and apply to ACAT for review, within 20 working days of the decision. A subdivision design application is a DA for creating or consolidating blocks or roads and is significant development with a 60 working day timeframe.

references.extracted_text: [Summary, not the source's wording] Application for development approval: $147.02 up to $1,500 cost of works, then a base fee plus a percentage, for example $1,121.36 plus 0.585% over $150,000 for $150,001 to $250,000, and $1,747.00 plus 0.438% over $250,000 for $250,001 to $500,000. Single residential DA amendment $382.71 plus notification. Reconsideration $413.08. Exemption declaration for a non-compliant single dwelling $728.96. Lease variation, consolidation or subdivision $2,732.33 plus $362.02 per additional component. Unit titling of a two-unit residential development $2,851.52. Certificate of Occupancy and Use $361.53. Building levy 1.40% of the cost of class 1 and 2 work, 1.28% for other work, plus a training levy of 0.2% for work of $10,000 or more. Pre-lodgement meeting: nil.

rule_sets.title: ACT: houses and extensions
rule_sets.description: Development application or exemption, building approval and certificate of occupancy for houses, extensions and secondary residences.
limitations: We don't know your zone, your crown lease or the development controls for your block, so we can't say whether your project is exempt, only which approvals you may need.
The Territory Plan's zone policies and the Planning (Exempt Development) Regulation 2023 are not encoded. ACTmapi shows your zone and overlays.
Constraints like heritage and bushfire come from your answers. Not ticking one doesn't mean it doesn't apply.
Not legal advice. Confirm with ACT Planning, a building certifier or a town planner before you rely on it.

rules.title: A development application may be needed, unless the work is exempt

outcomes.title: You may need a development application (DA)
outcomes.detail: In the ACT many single houses and extensions are exempt from a DA if they meet every criterion in the Planning (Exempt Development) Regulation 2023, like setbacks, height, the crown lease and neighbour notification. If they don't, you lodge a DA on eDevelopment. A standard DA is decided in 30 working days, or 45 if neighbours comment. Ask your building certifier for a formal exemption notice if you think it's exempt.

approval.pathway: Development approval under the Planning Act 2023, assessed against the Territory Plan

evidence.title: Site plan with setbacks, heights and existing buildings

payload.task: Ask your building certifier whether the work is exempt from a DA

rules.notes: MAY_APPLY because exempt status depends on criteria we don't collect.

rules.title: Building work needs building approval from a private certifier

outcomes.title: You likely need building approval from a private certifier
outcomes.detail: Most building work in the ACT needs building approval under the Building Act 2004, even when it is exempt from a DA. You appoint a licensed building surveyor as your certifier. They assess the plans, issue the building approval and the commencement notice, and inspect the work. You pay the building levy (1.40% of the cost of a house) and the training levy (0.2% for work of $10,000 or more), plus the certifier's own fee.

approval.authority: A private licensed building surveyor (building certifier) you appoint
approval.pathway: Building approval under the Building Act 2004 (National Construction Code)

rules.title: A certificate of occupancy and use at the end

outcomes.title: You will need a certificate of occupancy and use before you move in
outcomes.detail: When you apply for building approval you nominate the kind of certificate of occupancy you will apply for. Once the work is finished and your certifier has done the final inspection, the certificate is issued. The fee is $361.53 (2026-27). Don't move in or use the building before you have it.

approval.authority: Construction Occupations Registrar (Access Canberra), after your certifier's final inspection
approval.pathway: Certificate of occupancy and use under the Building Act 2004

payload.task: Nominate the certificate of occupancy type on your building approval application

rules.notes: Whether every extension needs a new certificate was not confirmed.

rules.title: ACT Heritage Register places

outcomes.title: Heritage listing means you likely need a DA
outcomes.detail: If your place is on the ACT Heritage Register, or near one, the work is unlikely to be exempt. Your DA is referred to the ACT Heritage Council, and a proposal likely to have a significant adverse impact on a heritage place may need an environmental impact statement. Talk to ACT Planning before you design.

approval.pathway: Development approval under the Planning Act 2023, assessed against the Territory Plan

payload.task: Check the ACT Heritage Register and ask ACT Planning for pre-DA advice

rules.notes: Heritage is a general exemption criterion; Heritage Register page not read this session.

rules.title: Bushfire prone blocks

outcomes.title: You must build to a bushfire attack level
outcomes.detail: Rural areas in the ACT are declared bushfire prone, and some urban blocks have bushfire construction requirements too. Your building must meet the Bushfire Attack Level (BAL) in AS 3959-2018 set by the development controls or your DA conditions. A DA may require a site-specific BAL assessment by a bushfire consultant. Your certifier checks this.

payload.task: Ask your certifier which BAL applies to your block

rules.title: Protected trees

outcomes.title: Trees on or near your block can stop work being exempt
outcomes.detail: Tree protection is one of the general criteria for exempt development in the ACT. If your work could damage a protected tree, you may need a DA and tree approval. Ask ACT Planning or an arborist early.

approval.pathway: Development approval under the Planning Act 2023, assessed against the Territory Plan

payload.task: Check for protected trees before you design

rules.notes: Tree Protection Act details not read this session.

rules.title: Easements

outcomes.title: Building over an easement can stop work being exempt
outcomes.detail: Easements are one of the general criteria for exempt development. Building on or over one usually needs a DA and the service owner's consent.

rules.title: Secondary residences need a DA

outcomes.title: You likely need a development application
outcomes.detail: A single house is only exempt when it is the only dwelling on the block, so a secondary residence (granny flat) needs a DA. You also need building approval from a certifier.

approval.pathway: Development approval under the Planning Act 2023, assessed against the Territory Plan

payload.task: Lodge a DA for the secondary residence on eDevelopment

rules.title: Secondary residences are limited to 90 m2

outcomes.title: At 90 m2 or less, your granny flat fits the size limit
outcomes.detail: The Residential Zones Policy limits a secondary residence to 90 m2. It must also be single level, the only secondary residence on the block, and on a block over 500 m2.

payload.task: Check your block is over 500 m2 and the design is single level

outcomes.title: Over 90 m2, it isn't a secondary residence
outcomes.detail: A secondary residence can't be larger than 90 m2. A bigger second home is a dual occupancy, which has different rules. On an RZ1 block over 800 m2, a second dwelling of up to 120 m2 may be allowed and unit titled. Get planning advice.

payload.task: Reduce the size to 90 m2 or get advice on a dual occupancy

rules.title: Block must be over 500 m2

outcomes.title: Your block is over 500 m2
outcomes.detail: In the RZ1 zone a secondary residence needs a block over 500 m2. Check your zone on ACTmapi; other residential zones have their own rules.

outcomes.title: Your block may be too small for a secondary residence
outcomes.detail: In the RZ1 zone a secondary residence is only allowed on a block over 500 m2. Check your zone on ACTmapi and ask ACT Planning.

rules.notes: Rules for zones other than RZ1 not confirmed.

rules.title: Secondary residences can't be sold separately

outcomes.title: You can't sell a secondary residence separately
outcomes.detail: A secondary residence can't be separately titled or sold. Since 27 November 2023, a different option exists on RZ1 blocks over 800 m2: a dual occupancy with a second dwelling of up to 120 m2, which can be unit titled and sold. If it is larger than 120 m2 it can't be unit titled.

rules.notes: Dual occupancy unit titling read from an Assembly question summary; confirm against the Residential Zones Policy.

rules.title: Your crown lease may need varying

outcomes.title: Your crown lease may only allow one dwelling
outcomes.detail: Many ACT crown leases allow one dwelling. If yours does, you need a lease variation as well as the DA. The application fee is $2,732.33 (2026-27). A Lease Variation Charge may also apply: the charge for an extra dwelling is set by suburb and can be large. Ask the Leasing Team whether a remission applies to secondary residences.

approval.pathway: Variation of a crown lease under the Planning Act 2023, with any Lease Variation Charge

payload.task: Check the purpose clause of your crown lease

rules.notes: Whether the Lease Variation Charge applies to secondary residences was not confirmed.

rules.title: Subdividing or unit titling

outcomes.title: You need approval to subdivide or unit title
outcomes.detail: In the ACT, land is leased from the Territory. Creating new blocks needs a subdivision design application, a significant DA decided in 60 working days. Splitting an existing residential block with two dwellings is usually done by unit titling, which needs approval and costs $2,851.52 for two units (2026-27). A lease variation ($2,732.33) and a Lease Variation Charge may also apply.

approval.pathway: Subdivision design application (significant development) or lease variation and unit titling under the Planning Act 2023 and Unit Titles Act 2001

rules.title: Lease variation and the Lease Variation Charge

outcomes.title: Budget for a lease variation and possibly the Lease Variation Charge
outcomes.detail: Subdividing or consolidating usually means varying the crown lease. The application fee is $2,732.33 plus $362.02 per extra component (2026-27). If the variation adds value, for example more dwellings, a Lease Variation Charge may be payable before the lease is varied. Lease variation approvals end if the lease isn't varied within 2 years.

approval.pathway: Variation of a crown lease under the Planning Act 2023, with any Lease Variation Charge

outcomes.title: Bushfire requirements affect subdivision design
outcomes.detail: On bushfire prone land, the ACT Emergency Services Agency may be a referral entity and new blocks may need bushfire construction levels. Design for this from the start.

rules.title: A change of use may need a lease variation

outcomes.title: Check your crown lease purpose clause first
outcomes.detail: In the ACT, the crown lease says what a block can be used for. If the new use isn't allowed by your lease, you need a lease variation, which is a DA ($2,732.33 application fee, 2026-27), and a Lease Variation Charge may apply. Small home businesses can be exempt within limits on staff, floor area and vehicles.

approval.pathway: Variation of a crown lease under the Planning Act 2023, with any Lease Variation Charge
